utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Could I remind you of the affirmation you made which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, I want to clarify something that was said last night. On our page, it's 82, line 22. It's to do with the 20th when you return to the hangar -- or I say "return," you go to the hangar, clearly there is an incident, and you are asked the following question: "In accordance with your testimony, you, together with that captain, managed to introduce some order at the Ovcara hangar; is that correct?" And the answer that you gave was: "I introduced order at the hangar, thanks to commander Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "He is who ought to be credited with that more than anybody else, and of course his men and the soldiers that were there." Are you actually meaning Vujovic or do you mean Vojnovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. I just ask you who is it you're saying is responsible for that act, that they should be credited? Is it Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when we were resolving the problem with his men, then Vujovic should be credited for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But am I not right in saying that it is Vujovic who was convicted in Belgrade for the murder of these people? That's right, isn't it? You see for my part, I thought you'd said Vojnovic, not Vujovic. So the person you say should be credited is the very man who is responsible for the murder of those people that late evening; is that right? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he killed people. I know that he was held responsible for that. But what I also know is that at that point in time, he assisted me in the sense that he insisted that his men leave the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So he insisted that his men leave the hangar and that the prisoners were locked up in a secure location; is that it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I insisted on that and he helped me to achieve that, to get these people out so that the men inside would be safe and indoors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the men weren't safe indoors. They were murdered in the most dreadful way by this man and his gang that very same day, the man you say should be given credit.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that happened later, and I cannot analyse his conduct after that. I neither knew what he did nor what his contribution in that event was. This was something established by court and he was sentenced, but I'm telling you about that particular moment. At that particular moment, he helped me by insisting that his men leave the hangar; and in that sense, I was assisted by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you use the word "credited," does that not in some ways -- is that not rather offensive just on a -- in a perceptive way? Crediting a man who is responsible for rounding up and ensuring that individuals are locked and then murdered by the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not trying to suggest an answer, but I think that the witness was clear about his position about Vujovic at the point in time when he was with him, not about the knowledge of what happened afterwards, which is what Mr. Moore is putting to him now. The witness is talking about the moment in time when he was with him, and Mr. Moore wants him to speculate. I don't need to comment any further, but I think that it's clear what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will move on to a slightly different topic, and it's quite simply this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told, I think, Mr. Vasic, that the violence at Ovcara was much worse than at the barracks. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that violence was by Vujovic's men, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move back to some of your interviews. We have seen the interview yesterday at tab 1 and 2, 16th of November. I want to deal with tab 3 and 4. 4 is the B/C/S, tab 3 is the English, 21st of December. So it is five weeks after you had already been interviewed by the military prosecutor. Now, while the file is being obtained, would it be right to say that you spoke to others about your testimony and/or what had happened at Ovcara prior to this investigating judge of the military court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So any alteration in the account that you gave was a result of your reflection, your individual and independent reflection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, shall we just look at it? I'm going to use the same system. I will try and refer to page numbers. The first thing is you clearly were informed that you were not obliged to answer any particular questions, if it is probable that in such a way, you may expose yourself or any close relative to deep disgrace, material damage, or criminal prosecution, and that you were obliged to speak the truth and that you must not be silent on any issue, and then you were warned that giving a false statement was a crime, and then there was a matter about change of address. The first paragraph basically relates to your background. I don't want to really deal with that. English page 3 of 7. Now, it's for you, it is the very bottom of page 0218-8283. So let's just look at this. The sentence starting: "Pursuant to those assignments on the 18th of November, 1991." Have you got that particular passage?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. "I was ordered by Major Sljivancanin to provide the buses for evacuation for a number of persons from the hospital in Vukovar, acting accordance to the given order on the 19th/11th around 6.00 in the morning," and I accept 19th to the 20th. "I headed to the Vukovar Hospital with six coaches. When I arrived to the hospital, I found there Major Sljivancanin, Major Karan, and Captain Karanfilov, as well as the commander of the military police company, Simic, whose unit was guarding the hospital in Vukovar." So in this was December 1998, Karanfilov has now been located by you at the hospital. That is right, isn't it? That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You then go on and say: "There is Paunovic, commander of the military police battalion. He was securing the hospital. At the hospital, performed was triage of all the persons found there, in accordance with some categories, which I did not take part in. However, I was ordered by Major Sljivancanin to take all persons, single out in one group consisting of approximately 250, 260 people with the buses to the Vukovar barracks. For those who were singled out, I learned they were not ill or injured, but were the locals from Vukovar that had been engaged in combat activities against our units. While for some of them, I heard the stories that they had committed crimes which had to be checked." And then it goes on: "I noticed that there was a great deal" -- sorry, "there was a great number of the Territorial Defence members from the Petrova Gora detachment around the hospital. They were mainly the local people from Vukovar, who had known them well, and were very determined to single out particular persons in order to take some actions against them. We encountered many problems trying to stop them to single out anyone from the group. I did not specially count those separated. But according to the number, the buses, I transported them -- them in could take on, my guess was there could be around 250-260 people." So you would refer --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before you start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Mr. Moore proceeds with his question, I just wanted to say this: In the original version, I don't know -- I don't have the English translation. But in the line now quoted by Mr. Moore, line -- page 5, line 3, in the original text, it says, "I received a task from Major Sljivancanin." And then page 5, line 18, in the original, it says, "I received a task from Major Sljivancanin." In both cases, the original says "received a task;" whereas, the English translation reads "I was ordered." I just wanted to point your attention to this fact. Task or assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you, then, please, about the reference to the -- some categories. I presume that translation is correct. What were the categories at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the people who were there? There were people who were sick, wounded, and those who did not belong to the hospital. Those were the categories: Sick, wounded, and those neither sick nor wounded, but were staying at the hospital illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think you told us yesterday that in actual fact you had intelligence about various individuals who might have been desirable to be spoken to; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security service received information that there were certain groups in the hospital which, following the fall of Vukovar, took off their uniforms, discarded their weapons, and entered the hospital in order to become part of the convoy for the sick and wounded and flee from Vukovar. That's a fact. We received this information from our superior command, and we also knew this based on the work that we had performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's also right to say you had certain names; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any names, but most likely the security service, the security department had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's just move on to compare what your evidence was and what you say here. "I noticed that there was a great deal of the Territorial Defence members Petrova Gora detachment around the hospital." Now, what do you mean by the phrase: "They were very determined to single out particular persons in order to take some actions against them?"

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His presence was obvious and the way they behaved; they were shouting, yelling, whistling, and it all indicated that they knew those people there. But right there on the spot, there was nothing more but verbal protests, verbal displeasure that they exhibited, and that was aimed at certain individuals. There was no other physical violence nor there could have been at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the word and phrase is "very determined." What is that supposed to mean? Because I'd suggest it's more than just whistling and shouting names. So why do you use the phrase "very determined" to single out particular persons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are concluding that based on the translation. It was my assessment that their presence and their conduct hinted at the possibility that there could be such behaviour. Yes. There was a possibility for that. But at that point in time, on that spot, there was no violence whatsoever, nor was there any possibility for any violence to be exhibited. It was just my personal assessment that based on their conduct and based on their appearance, there was a potential for that, if you are following me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that was outside the hospital grounds in full view of everyone; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside of the hospital compound, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in view of everyone and able to be heard by virtually everyone; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were there were able to hear that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just move on to the next paragraph. It deals with the transfer of 150 people. Pursuant to the English order - obviously, as Mr. Lukic would say "task" - issued by Major Sljivancanin, you thought maybe it would be Sid, then there's reference to Predojevic, and then I'd like to commence if I may, please, with: "There was also here in the barracks yard a great number of members of the Petrova Gora Territorial Defence detachment who attempted using aggressive ruthless methods to separate some people from the bus and to take them under their charge in order to clear up the things with them. We prevented them in that; frequently exposed to verbal abuses, unpleasantness and even reaching for their guns." Now, are you happy enough with the translation, Mr. Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's the same people from the Petrova Gora, that's correct, isn't it, that you saw at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "Using aggressive and ruthless methods to separate some people from the bus." Please tell us what aggressive and ruthless methods they were attempting to use to separate people and take them away.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aggressivity that I described at the time, the aggressiveness that I described at the time manifested itself in their verbal threats, pointing out to individuals, threatening gestures, and cursing. They were unable to get on the buses. They were milling around the buses, and the only avenue open to them was to recognise say their neighbour, who, in their view, was guilty. So they were making threatening gestures showing that they would slaughter them, because everything else was not allowed to them. So in that sense, it was the -- that type of aggressive behaviour and threats aimed at intimidating the people. This is how I describe their aggressive behaviour. I said that they wanted to settle accounts with certain people that they considered guilty because they had recognised their neighbours, if I understood your question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we have heard evidence here, and I'll see if I can assist by way of recollection. Did you see people with knives out and waving knives? The answer is yes or no, surely?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Because we have had evidence from some of the people in the buses that knives were being waved and even drawing across the throat clearly indicating that throats would be cut. You've probably seen that on television, occasionally. Did you see anything like that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw weapons, but I didn't see knives. I saw weapons, yes. I saw weapons pointed, weapons held in hands. But as for knives, I can't that I saw them when I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, what weapons did you see pointed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their weapons, the weapons that they had on them. Those were our automatic rifles, pistols, stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when the use the phrases you did a couple of minutes ago,"showing them that they would slaughter them," that clearly indicates, I would suggest, that if they had got hold of them, there was an intention to kill them. I see there's another problem with the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never heard the witness said that they would slaughter them. He said that they threatened with their fingers as though they would kill them. If it was a case of bad translation, then I apologise for not reacting earlier, if that is indeed how it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Some of the distinctions in translation that you draw, Mr. Lukic, are extremely fine, bearing in mind the capacity in each language for different expressions to convey a meaning. The interpreters try to give the sense of what is being said, rather than, as I understand it, a mechanical exactly precise translation where that is possible. Often it is not, and the nearest words have to be used. So I wouldn't think at this point, that that interpretation or translation requires correction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It meant quite simply this, didn't it, that if they had got hold of them, they were indicating, whether, it was right or not, that they would kill them. That's the phrase you use, even by Mr. Lukic's translation. That's right, isn't it, Mr. Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that. You're drawing conclusions, and you're doing it presently. I don't see based on what should I have concluded that. I never said that I knew they would kill them. I said that they acted aggressively, that they sought out their neighbours, that they threatened them. And as for killing them, that was your conclusion, not mine. And in addition to that, they were unavailable to them. What do you say? They were available to them. Had they been available to them, yes, they would have done it right there on the spot, but we didn't allow them to do what you said, to kill them right away. Please don't turn your conclusions into practical consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I merely use your words. But I will move on, as a result of one of the things you have said. "Had they been available to them, yes, they would have done it right there on the spot." The fact of the matter is, they were available to them, and you became aware of that fact later on that day; isn't that right? I presume you agree with that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. I absolutely disagree with your conclusion, and please don't put me in the position where I do not belong. I am responsible only for those instance where I was present. You have tried several times to impute that I had done certain things which I didn't. I would like to kindly ask you to treat me fairly and to have a proper exchange with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Firstly, I would suggest to you I'm being perfectly fair, and I'm using the words that you use. You may not like them and you may not like the way the question is framed, but I am only using your words, Mr. Vukasinovic. Do we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well let's see about that. For the time being, I do not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us look at the next paragraph. "While I was in the barracks, I received a list of the part of the persons from these buses," then there's reference to 20, it came from Sljivancanin, "told me to separate them and return them to the hospital." "I experienced many difficulties with reference to the behaviour of the Territorial Defence members about which I told you a while ago," and indeed you did here. "Major Sljivancanin tasked me to release those persons who are going brought back to the hospital which I did." And then there is reference to the fact that what I will call the reselection, "It was local people and hospital staff had intervened for them, that they found at the hospital by accident and could not be held responsible for whatsoever. So there was no need to treat them specially." Well, the first thing I want to ask you is this: Did you have a radio or a method of electronic communication with you when you were at the barracks? And please bear in mind that evidence has been given prior to you giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question. Did I have what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you have a radio? Sometimes it's called a Motorola. Did you have access to a radio?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, I didn't have a radio in the car.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer, the interpreters didn't understand what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You're being asked to repeat your reply as there's difficulty with interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have a Motorola with me, and I was unable to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We heard from Mr. Simic that he had access at the barracks to a radio. Did you attempt to use a radio or find out if a radio was available at the forward command post? If I've said Simic, I meant Susic. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was radio communication; there's no doubt about that. I don't know what radio communication has got to do with me when we're referring to the 20 people. We are discussing this, and now you are asking me about radio communication. Radio communication did exist in the OG South. We had radio communication with the OKM and IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The reason I ask you about a radio is that with a radio, you have the ability to contact Sljivancanin, who had a radio. We know that; he's told us that. You would be in a position to tell him the situation at the barracks, and you would be in a position to tell him about the difficulties that you were encountering, wouldn't you? And also, by the way, to send a bus up.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained to Major Sljivancanin when I returned with the 20 people about the situation at the barracks, because it wasn't something that he wasn't aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you gave this statement, there is no reference, as far as I can see, about the reselection process, where Mr. Sljivancanin went along asking them individual questions assisted by, I think it was, Vujanovic and perhaps members of the TO. Is there any why it's not in there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next paragraph. The reference is: "In the second go, I took the remaining people, singled out in the military hospital in Vukovar, taking them around 1400 hours to the Vukovar barracks." Then you inform -- or are informed by Captain Predojevic what had happened and that the commander had given an order that they be taken to Ovcara. So it's very similar to the evidence that you have given here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question that I have for you is this: If you took them to the Vukovar barracks at 1400 hours, as you say, that means that the ICRC and the ECMM have been at the Vukovar Hospital for something close to three and a half hours, while this group of people who had been isolated were presumably sitting in a bus or were about to be selected. Am I right on my timings on that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, I said where was this group in the hospital. They were in the buses. I was very precise about that. And that I arrived with that group to Ovcara at around 1300, 1330. That was my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, here you see, you're saying quite simply, you're taking them around 2.00 in the afternoon to the Vukovar barracks. And my point, and it's a point that everyone in this room is aware of, is we have heard tranches of evidence, large amounts of evidence that those people were moved in one group, and they were out of the hospital before the monitors arrived. Now, your account is that this group was split into two, and that the final group only left on this account around about 1.00 in the afternoon. I mean that's your evidence, isn't it, without beating about the bush?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I claim that there were two groups, not one. I may vary the times up to one or half an hour, but what I stated is true; first one group and then the second group. What is not true is that there was just one column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And let's just take your account. There are therefore three buses, two of them full of men, with armed guards, and a third bus with five or six on board sitting outside the hospital for three and a half hours when the ICRC and the ECMM monitors are there. That's, in reality, what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived, I found two buses; and the one which I emptied which had several people on it, that was my second column of buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And on your account, the reselection process with Sljivancanin involved and the TOs with Vojnovic asking questions occurred while the monitors were there. That's also what you're saying; is that right? That's your account.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I describe the work to release these people, and at the moment the monitors were not there while that was being done. While we were going about releasing these people, I did not see a single ECMM member next to Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Look, all I want to know is, simple question: Are you saying the monitors were there prior to your return from the barracks? Now, simple question; yes or no, please. You know, they are the men who used to be called the ice cream men in the white suits. That was the phrase that was often given to them.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned from the barracks, they were there at the hospital. When I returned with 20 people, they were there at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And therefore, on your account, the reselection process which took an hour, approximately, the reselection process was being done in the hospital grounds; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the reselection process was being done where?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in that, and I cannot say anything about that to you. I stated that I had no knowledge of that. I wasn't there, and I don't know where or when the process of triage was being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the small group of people, the 20 that you brought back. Are you saying you weren't present when that was done, or you weren't aware?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently, we cannot understand each other, and we do not want to understand each other. Listen, you are asking me about the triage -- well, now you say that I returned pursuant to a list, 20 people back. We are not talking about triage. We are discussing the -- their involvement in combat on their status, whether they were innocent, righteous people or people taking part in combat. This is what we discussed. And there were guarantees about these people in the conversation with Major Sljivancanin that they were clean, that they had not fought, and that they just took refuge in the hospital, and that was the basis for him releasing a number of people. This is not a triage. This was an attempt to establish some facts, so that we could do the right thing. Let's understand one another. When we say triage, then this is the triage at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the 20 people who were brought back -- I call this, for convenience, a reselection process. All right? Because people are being selected, either -- for whatever reason, off they go to the barracks, and 20 are brought back. So to try and distinguish, I call this a reselection process. So the 20 people come back, and I want to know where this reselection process occurred? What location?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, that was in front of the gatehouse, on the entrance to the hospital. It was a wider space next to that gate house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that was being done when the monitors were at the hospital; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probable. This is not known to me. I know that they were there. They were not over there; they were supposed to be at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have seen video clips of the ECM monitors there; they were gentlemen in white suits. I was not trying to trivialise it in any way. I want a simple answer, I believe to a simple question: When those 20 people were brought back, are you saying that the monitors were there or were not there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And therefore, on your account, this reselection process of 20 men, with the TOs assisting Sljivancanin, was being done in front of -- when the monitors were there. That is what you are saying; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, they were not immediately there, but they were within the hospital. But they were not in the immediate vicinity of this process of reselection or triage. Nobody of them was standing there. I don't know what you want me to tell you. I'm telling you what happened and where it happened, but now you want me to say that they were there. They were not there in the immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. I suggest you are merely telling us what you believe happened. I am suggesting that that triage, if it is that, or a reselection process, occurred at a time when the monitors were not there, and that all these men were out and away before the monitors were let in at 10.00 to 10.30 by Mr. Sljivancanin. That's what I'm suggesting.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that. I know when I set out, and I know what they were doing there in front of -- so I could not agree with such a statement. I don't know when they -- exactly they entered, but I know that it was after 1100 hours when this triage, as you put it, the triage of the 20 people was taking place. It was after 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moore, I detect you've reached an end of a subject for a moment so I turn to Mr. Lukic. Do you have an objection? There was a subject theme that I wanted to see finished before we took the objection. There is nothing to be pursued. It's been cleared up, so carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we go to your page 0218-8285. I want to deal with this area of evidence. It is page 4 of 7 of the English version, four-fifths of the way down the page in the middle. It starts as follows: "The hangar was guarded by one MP platoon, a part of a unit from ..." and then it goes on the 80th Brigade, do you see that? "I think the commander was Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic." So it should be your page 0218-8285. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no such page here. There are two 284 but not 285.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will read out what I've got, and you can assist us. It's not a large part. I think what you'll find is the page number has not got a good number on it. It's been covered by photo copying. If you look at it, it's between 83 and 85. Can you do that? Mr. Lukic has an objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, no, he's eager to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's page 4 of your statement before the military court at the beginning, as far as I understood what Mr. Moore was trying to say, when Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic is mentioned. Can you see that, Mr. Vukasinovic? The first paragraph, the first line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have we got that? The real key is, "I believe it was the 80th Brigade ..."

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your read it out; I will listen to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to make sure that you have it. It makes life so much easier. Have you got it there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go on, read it, please, and I will be listening to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. It goes on about Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. "The persons brought by me were put in a hangar with my presence, and no one did undertake any actions that would present physical abuse or maltreating." And then you say you don't know whether it referred to the previous group, because you were not there. "I do not have any knowledge if someone was fully abusing them while putting them in the hangar. All those people placed in this hangar, how much I knew there was supposed to stay there for one day as the longest in order to do some checks and to take them to Sid or Sremska Mitrovica, which was done with the previously-captured persons." The next, 5 of 7: "At Ovcara, I found then Lieutenant-Colonel Panic. He was the assistant brigade commander. I did not know the reasons why he was here. I did not contact him. I simply noticed him here, but he left shortly after that." Now, yesterday, you told us that you did speak to Panic; and indeed, you were angry with Mr. Panic. I'm not saying you had a healthy discussion with him, but you spoke to him; isn't that right? That's what your evidence here is. But in this, you say you didn't contact him, you simply noticed him. Can you just explain the distinction in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is in this: I approached him. It wasn't a conversation; I just asked him: "Why are these people here?" Because I saw that this wasn't part of my task. When I saw the Chief of Staff, it was only natural for me to ask him what people, which had no need to be there, were doing there. He just looked at me and said, "It was so ordered," and then he left. This is a minute or maybe a couple of seconds of -- worth of conversation that I had with him and nothing more; and, of course, my answer is dependent on the questions put to me. Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was a witness. You could ask him what his answer was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question I'm asking you is: How is it that you say that you don't say anything here when you're speaking in 1998; and yet when you give your evidence, you are concerned and angry? Because, after all, he is the Chief of Staff, isn't he, superior rank to you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the Chief of Staff, that is correct. He is my superior in the chain of command, and that is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the evidence that you gave was quite specific in the nature of your concern, wasn't it? Because you said to him, "What is this? Who ordered this?" And then you went to the hangar to see what was going on. So in actual fact, I would suggest the whole thrust of that is you're going to Panic himself, that you are very unhappy because you are angry with him, you told us that. And what is this? Who ordered this? It goes to the whole crux, doesn't it? It goes to behaviour, it goes to control, it goes to why are they in Ovcara? It deals with the core of the whole case. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My question to Panic was addressed for exactly that reason, because the task I was given took a turn in the direction; and as second in command, he was supposed to give me an answer. And in that sense, I addressed him with a single sentence to see where did this change in the direction of the task came from. And then I turned to set off towards the hangar to see what was going on. But still, I was performing this basic function of transferring those separated people and protecting them. I didn't deal with other business. I dealt with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, you are coming to this court. You are sitting there and you're saying: I am an honest man. I am here to tell the truth. That's what you're saying, isn't it? I was there, you weren't; I know what happened, you didn't. That's what it's all about, isn't it. And I'm asking you how it is when you're asked in December about Panic, you say: I didn't contact him. And yet when you come here to this Bench and everyone here, you are irritated, you are angry with your Chief of Staff, what's going on, who did this? And I'm saying to you that's an extremely important question, and I want to know what your answer is. Why you didn't mention it in December in 1998? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm telling you, I mentioned that only when asked about it. I simply, in my first statement, the question was: Who did you see there? I said I saw Panic, Chief of Staff. It depends on the investigating judge's level of detail sought by him. I answered his question. At this place, I'm saying what should be said, what I omitted before which I remembered in the meantime. This is the right place to tell the right truth, and this is why I'm here. And as you say, I am an honest man; I can say that with full fright. If I'm who not an honest man, somebody is going to disprove me. But this is my right to say and contend that I am an honest man. I don't know what you have against my attitude. We are discussing about events and not who is an honest man and who isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it might be honesty is something a Court has to take into account. Are you aware that Susic has given evidence, and indeed others have given evidence at various times, saying that a colonel went out with the convoy from the JNA barracks. But nobody seems to be able to identify him. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've never heard the fact that a colonel and a TO captain were responsible -- no, wrong, that a colonel and a TO captain went out in a separate vehicle with the buses on the way to Ovcara? You never heard that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the statement of an eye witness. I did not see that, and I cannot confirm anything. If he saw that, he stated that. That's his statement. What I know, I'm going to testify about. But please do not lead me into saying something that I don't know. Whether a colonel was there, I don't know. If Mr. Susic cannot recognise a colonel, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, when you were at the barracks, reflecting upon what you had seen there, give us the names of any colonels you saw there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see a single colonel in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us move on, then, to the next paragraph. There is reference about "as soon as combat actions stopped ..." Sorry, my apologies, the next one relates to Petrova Gora. So it's Petrova Gora again. So it's the people who were threatening at the hospital, the people who were threatening at the buses, and it's the Petrova Gora again at Ovcara. That is correct, isn't it, along with others, obviously. That's right, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find this passage that you are reading. Could you please tell me, is that the statement -- am I reading the right statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to start again.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Belgrade court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, just listen to me for a moment, please, all right? Thank you very much. If you go to tab 4. Have you got tab 4? The tabs are on the right-hand side. Have you got tab 4?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, find page 0218-8285.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that page; I keep telling you that. I don't have the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Find page 8286. They are at the top right-hand corner. Everybody else, I think, has got them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 8286. Have you got that, Mr. Vukasinovic? Top right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well turn back one page, and that's 8285. Have you got that page?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Turn back one page, and you've got 8284. So I want you -- you've got 8285; I want you to go back to 8284. Right. Now you've been shown by the legal assistant. I want you to deal with the paragraph: "While I was in the barracks ..." Have you got that? I really want to move on a bit quicker if I can?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just confirm that what you say in 1998, that you're saying that you see the same group, the Petrova Gora; the same group that you had seen at the barracks, the same groups that you'd seen at the hospital, and now the same group are at Ovcara; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you agree with that as being accurate; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group moved. I was unable to recognise all of them; but, generally speaking, that group moved as I moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So we have got the same people. Now, let us move on to 8285. Have you got that page?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to deal with halfway down the page. It refers to the sentence; it's 5 of 7 in English: "After placing those people in hangars, I returned back to my command post." Have you got that? It's the penultimate paragraph, by the looks of it. "After placing those people in hangars, I returned back to my command post." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's read it, please. "After placing those people in hangars, I returned back to my command post. After that, on the 19th," which is the 20th, "around 2130, Major Sljivancanin and I went to the Ovcara agricultural farm in order to inspect the sector, on which occasion one of the officers, who was participating in guarding those detained in the hangars, handed over a report to Major Sljivancanin informing him that there had been no problems. We stayed there for about 20 minutes, unable to notice anything strange. "Everything was all right. Besides, we also were there to see whether there were any attempts of robbery since we had that information, as well as to see if there was some other problems arising from guarding those detained persons. Personally, I noticed on that occasion a number of Petrova Gora territorial unit members strolling around that area even though it was dark, but I noticed that it was them. They did not do anything at that time, nor the duty officer informed us about that. "After approximately 20 minutes, two of us returned to our command post. After we returned from Ovcara that evening, I believe that Major Sljivancanin informed Commander Mrksic about our observations. I had no obligations or duties that would refer to those people placed in the hangar in Ovcara. My next engagement was on the assignments of a different nature. However, during the 20th," obviously the 21st of November, "news spread out that the persons placed in the hangar at Ovcara were either disappeared and killed." Now I want to deal with this account, which I suggest is very similar to the account that you gave, but with variations on a them, if I may use that phrase. The visit that you went to Ovcara, whatever date it was, the visit in the evening was at approximately 9.30; is that right? Whether it was the actual 19th or the actual 20th, the time was 9.30, there or thereabouts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2130, that would be the time, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if it was the 19th or the 20th, in relation, you only stayed 20 minutes, and you were back in the Negoslavci area approximately 10.00ish; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely at about 10.00, we were back, because that's quite close and one doesn't need more time to get back, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so if it was the 19th, you went from Negoslavci with Sljivancanin, and you returned to Negoslavci with Sljivancanin; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Obviously to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I am -- what do you want me to say, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want you to answer the question. We know it's about Ovcara. If it is the 19th, the actual 19th or the actual 20th, that can be determined later. You are back in Negoslavci by 10.00, and you are probably out of Negoslavci a little bit before, let's say, 9.00. Would that be right? You are away from Negoslavci, the both of you, for about an hour, an hour and 15 minutes; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that we were absent for that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, it's not a question of possible. You're giving evidence. You say you remember it, and I'm asking you, you think it's 9.30. How long does it take to get from Negoslavci to Ovcara? Approximately, how long does it take?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So 15 minutes from Negoslavci to Ovcara, approximately 20 minutes, I'm not going to hold you on 20 minutes. Approximately, 20 minutes there, and 15 minutes back; yes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it was night-time, yes, and the road was clear, no traffic, then yes. I told you that already. I don't see why you keep insisting on time. We were there. Now as to the exact time, yes, it's within that time frame. I don't see the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so Sljivancanin goes back; and as far as you are aware, he speaks to Mrksic, what shall we say, 2200 hours? 2230?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I don't know whether he went to see Mrksic at all and, if so, when. I suppose that he did go to Mrksic, but I didn't go with him so I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, but you use the phrase: "I believe that Sljivancanin informed the commander about our observations."

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the observations were in relation to problems arising from guarding "those detained persons." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said there, and now when we translate it, then, yes, it is all consistent. But what I wanted to tell you is that I spent a -- lost a whole day when I was giving evidence and statements. On the 19th, I went to see civilians and the wounded. All of this was taking place in the same day. I don't know if you can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, you have told us that. I'm not trying to be discourteous in any way. I'm saying on the account that you gave to the court, it was in relation to reporting back for the problems arising from guarding those detained persons. That is correct, isn't it? That is correct.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I stated there, yes. That's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I deal, then, with your evidence -- sorry, I just want to go to the next page, and it's my fault for just dealing with it that way. Go to page 0218-8286. Have you got that? Top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I read in from the previous page: "However, during the 21st," although you say 20th, "news spread out that persons placed in the hangar near Ovcara were either disappeared and killed. I had no assignments whatsoever with reference to that nor had I the obligation to investigate if it really took place, from which reason, and who did it. As much as I know, no one from our unit command did verify that information. Furthermore, I do not know why it was done. I have heard only that during the night, they disappeared and most likely were killed. But who did it, I do not know." Now, let's do it in a slightly Irish way; let's start at the back and move forward. This is 1998. "But who did it, I do not know." Well, you may not actually know, because I'm not suggesting you were present at that time, but you had a pretty good idea who was the number one suspect, didn't you? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the question that was put to me then. And these were my thoughts with respect to that question, because I knew that members of the army would not do such things. And this is a reply that I gave to the question put to me by the judge, as to who might have done it. And I said that it could have been those who had acted that way all along, but under no circumstances could that be members of the army. I knew my men in my unit. I knew that my men and my officers in my unit would have never done that. That is my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am right in saying that you were aware the following day that, in actual fact, the suggestion was that either they had disappeared or been killed. That is correct, isn't it? That was your state of knowledge on the 21st of November. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know. I heard. Had I knew, I would have done something, but I didn't know. To know and to hear are two very different things. These are quite different claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And moving back again: "As much as I know, no one from our unit command did verify that information." Now, "no one from our unit command," who is your unit command? Can you just tell us who you're referring to there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command of the Guards Brigade, and that was my original basic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So that, presumably, means Mrksic; is that correct? Yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command of the unit, that's how it goes, in that sequence; Commander, Chief of Staff, and then down the chain of command. It is clear that Mrksic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware, Mrksic did nothing to verify that information; if, of course, he was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the right question. That's exactly the question that I put. Naturally, if he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Sljivancanin, he did nothing, of course, provided on his state of knowledge at the time; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, all of that is linked. You cannot have a situation where the top man and the chief of security know nothing, and how can they order things? Now, as to whether they knew or didn't know, it's up to them to say. I have no right, nor do I attempt to speak on their behalf. I don't know whether they knew or didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I just go back to your evidence. And you told us that Mr. Sljivancanin was going past to I think it was the command briefing. He had only a few seconds. You mentioned Ovcara. He went off, he came back, and he said well done - I'm sorry, I forget the name that he uses - well done to you. I knew I could trust you. You mentioned to him the incidents at Ovcara and presumably the barracks. That's right, isn't it? And Mr. Sljivancanin said -- just remind us again what he said. Something along the lines that he would probably have a look at it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And as far as you are aware, he never did. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, I don't know whether he did. I did not receive a reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I asked the question very simply: As far as you are aware, he never did. As far as you are aware. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I know we're six minutes early from the break. I was going to move on to a different topic and move away from the statements and hopefully move a little faster, but I will come back to the statements in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Moore. We will resume at a quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, I'm going to move away from statements for the moment and I will be dealing really with topics and they don't always follow in sequence, I apologise for that but it's not always easy to do so. I want to deal with the briefing of Mr. Sljivancanin on the 19th of November, so that is the topic I wish to deal with. Is that all right? Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you start, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, no guarantee. So, how many people were at the briefing with Mr. Sljivancanin when tasks were being given out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody from the security department were there, but I don't remember the figure. They should be counted. All of them were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that briefing itself, as a general rule, tended to occur after what I will call the Mrksic command briefing; would that be right or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the command briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if the command briefing was at, let us say - and I don't say it for any particular reason - if it was at 6.00 and it was finished at 7.00, what I will call the security organ briefing or Mr. Sljivancanin's briefing would be after that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that is what happened on the 19th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefing was every day when he was there around the same time, around 7.30 p.m., until the point when I went back to the command post on the 19th when I was appointed as head of the command post, and then I wasn't a part of the team that attended the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But on the 19th, you were there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What sort of tasks were given out by Mr. Sljivancanin on the evening of the 19th? Just give us a flavour of that, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given my task and then left the briefing. I wasn't there to listen to other tasks being given. I could not linger on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were there any tasks given before you left, apart from the one to yourself?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the first to be issued with a task, and then I was free to go. I had duties to attend to at my command post, and this is why I was the first to be given my task; and then he was left with the other officers and gave out tasks known to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But normally, when one has a briefing, the person giving the briefing will have what I will call a preamble indicating the nature of the tasks that are to be done in general, and then moving on to the specific allocation; do you understand?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that. The task of the rest of them was to provide security for the following day, to put security measures in place, to make sure that the evacuation of the sick and the wounded from the hospital can be carried out; and pursuant to such security measures, everybody was given their particular task. But I was the first to be given my task, and I asked him to be allowed to return to my command post, because I had other duties and for the purpose of me preparing myself for that task given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I know this may be slightly corny, but rather like an orange, the person giving the brief indicates what the general shape is going to be; and then the parts of the orange, the components, the sectors, are then given to the individual person. Do you see my analogy? It's not a very good one, but would that be right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the method of work in any process, not in this briefing. There is the general and main tasks, which is then further elaborated upon into parts, and everybody is given that part to perform. That's correct. I fully agree with you here in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Perhaps we can forget the orange. Let's move on to the numbers. Would it be right to say that the number of, approximately, 200 individuals were believed to be in the hospital and represented those who were not genuinely there? Would that be a fairly reasonable figure that was given out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That figure was not known, at the evening, you mean, nobody knew that figure. The following day, that figure emerged. Nobody knew how many members of which category were in the hospital. The hospital had been taken, and it still had to be determined. So that nobody was dealing with any figures or numbers. There was this main task. And the main task was to secure evacuation of the sick and wounded; and that all those who do not belong to the hospital, who are not part of the hospital staff, those who took refuge in the hospital, they had to be separated and determined their status, because they could influence the security and safety of the operation to secure the sick and the wounded. We did not know who was in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just -- oh, you did know who was in the hospital; you just weren't sure of their identity. Well, the reason I ask you that question is because we have got an operational log belonging to the 80th Motorised Brigade, a warning order from memory from 1800 hours on the 19th where it gives the figure of 200 people, HDZ and MUP, I can't remember exactly, were expected. And I'm just curious if you might know how that number -- where that number came from? That's the first point. The second thing is that a grave was dug, and I think 198 bodies were taken out of it. So I'm just curious if you would know where that figure came from on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that figure. I have nothing to do with the 80th Brigade. This is their operational log. I had no access to their log, and I know nothing of the information that you are dealing with. I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then I will move on to a different topic. The Mitnica evacuation, you have told us about communication coming into Mr. Sljivancanin from Vasiljevic, in respect of the exchange of prisoners, Croatian forces, and officers; do you remember that? You've told -- given us evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when one hears about the Mitnica evacuation, the phrase that is invariably used is the "Mitnica Battalion." Have you heard them called that? The suggestion being that they are soldiers, basically, the fighters?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is more of a Mitnica group for me. That would be the term that I used and which corresponds to what they were, the Mitnica group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to ask about the perception existing at that time of the people in the hospital, the HDZ, the MUP, and can I just use the phrase "Ustasha criminals." Did you ever hear the fact about Ustasha criminals being in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a time, while I was an operative, I had information and sources and data that the so-called defenders of Vukovar, or as they were labelled, the HDZ men, they took part in combat in pursuit of their goals. Whether they were criminals or not, well, it later was confirmed that there was some crime being committed. And when we received from our superior command a list of which criminals there were, it wasn't a large number, but there were names submitted to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The names submitted to you, was that before the evacuation or after the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who were they again, please, can you just remind us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know now who those people were. We concluded the procedure. There were people who were not sick. It was possible to establish that,; and then there were also people who had acknowledged that they had fought on the side of Croatian forces; and then there were people who kept silent and did not acknowledge anything. This is why this triage was conducted through interviews and other means. We tried to establish whether there were any other criminals among them and who were the criminals and who were mere combatants. It was just a matter of a procedure to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I am relying on what you have said: "It was later confirmed that there was some crime being committed; and then we received from our superior command a list of which criminals there were. It wasn't a large number, but there were names submitted to us." So it's a case of names being given to you. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that wasn't given to me. I did not have those names, nor was I -- nor could I have had such names, because such names were sent to the security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What do you mean by the "security department?"

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the chief. He was the one receiving information from the superior command, instructions and all; and then he forwarded it to his organs, to his assistant for counter-intelligence work, and to other officers depending on each officer was in the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And they were names of people who were perceived to be criminals; that is right, isn't it? That's right, Mr. Vukasinovic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep testing me. I didn't read these names. I didn't read their dossiers. Yes. There was a number of people regarding whom we knew, that they had committed crimes, that they were criminals, and that there was a possibility that they had not surrendered and could be found in the hospital. This is why the instruction was given for the situation to be looked into and to see whether any such persons in the hospital. According to our information, in the final operations, the hospital served as a facility where all of those who had remained in town, who had taken part in combat and had refused to surrender, changed their clothes and hid in the hospital. That was a fact that we had information about. We established that to be so and measures were taken to that end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I presume what you mean is measures were taken to identify them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's also right to say that there was a belief by the JNA that atrocities had been committed against Serbs. That is also correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Atrocities were committed against Serbs and against other citizens who did not accept their policies, if I may call them that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I then move on to another topic. You told us about intelligence, you told us about lists and documents, and you referred to surveillance, I believe - it may have been my phrase rather than you - the tapping of communications, wiretapping, as I call it. I think that was done, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were measures conducted in combat operations, and this is done by certain organs on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not criticising or trying to attribute blame. I am merely saying the JNA had the facility and, indeed, did listen into communication; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they had the facility of listening to us as well. We were one single army. We had gone through the same training; and then overnight, we split into two opposing sides. So our enemy was not unknown to us. No, our enemy were our colleagues who had gone to school with us. So the same methods and principles --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not disputing that, but I want to just focus, please, on what the JNA were doing at that time. It is not a criticism. It is merely a process of trying to find out exactly what was occurring. So, you were listening in or wiretapping; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, but our organs did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And they had the capacity to be able to listen to radio communication and telephone communication; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All kinds of communication: Radio, telephone, wire. All kinds of conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You may or may not know the answer to this question. If you don't, just say: "I don't know." Were you aware that there had been wiretaps or listening in to what I will call peace negotiations or what I call surrender negotiations towards the end of the third week in November?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us then move on to another area. You have told us that I believe on the 18th of November, in relation to the Mitnica evacuation, everybody was everywhere and certain people were taking their cars; and you, not you personally, but they were informed that Ovcara was an exit point. That is right, isn't it, and a number of cars ended up at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think again from memory, you said that the cars were to be left there with the keys left in -- with the keys; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, when one approaches the hangar at Ovcara, I assume that we agree with this. You go along eventually a straight road from the yellow house, and the Ovcara hangar is on the right-hand side; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you, in your mind's eye, just tell us where it was the cars were parked at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halfway between the yellow house and the hangar, there is a meadow on the right side, and this is where they were parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And they were cars belonging to, principally, private people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when the cars were left, what happened to the owners of those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The owners were transported in buses to wherever they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we know some of them didn't manage to get there. Was it also right to say that there was an ongoing problem of people coming to claim those cars? Whether they genuinely owned the cars or genuinely had a right to drive the car was open to question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was waiting for the answer.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened carefully, but I wouldn't agree with you about those people not coming back. Those who left on the buses, they left. The cars remained there, and the cars were protected. Nobody stole the cars. Later on, these cars were turned over to the collection centre at Velepromet, down to the last one. I remember that a yellow Mercedes had gone missing, and we found it in the course of the day and brought it back. So down to the last car, all of them were taken to the collection centre at Velepromet. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard the answer, but in Mr. Moore's question, this fact that was stated in the question is not something that we heard during the trial, that those who came on the 18th to Ovcara did not manage to leave, at least I'm not familiar with that reference; and if Mr. Moore can enlighten us, please go ahead. We know of only one testimony where something of the sort is mentioned, but this fact was not part of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I was trying to find out from the witness whether, in actual fact, he was aware if people were claiming their car or not claiming their car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can you assist us that they, firstly, were under guard; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That there was always the danger of someone coming to collect those cars; is that correct? I say "danger," there was always the likelihood of someone coming to collect those cars; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was danger, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And there was always a likelihood, it could either be a person who was genuinely entitled or perhaps someone who was pretending to be entitled?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the question is -- Mr. Moore, all kinds of unlawful things take place during the war. So anybody who came to claim the car and was not the lawful owner, that is considered theft. So the owners could come, yes; but in that sense, there was the danger. And this why we tried to protect the cars to ensure that they wouldn't be stolen. Now, as to who could have stolen them, that's a different question. Whether it was the citizens or those other ones who were there, that's questionable. But the fact is that it was dangerous for them to be piled up all in one place, and we didn't have enough forces to deal with all kinds of security issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, you missed my point. My point is quite simply this: That there was a likelihood that civilians would come to the Ovcara area to claim a car. That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. As to such assumptions, yes, we can reflect on them now; but at that time, who would come back when was quite uncertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's exactly the point I'm trying to make; that it was not known when someone would come to collect a car.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at Ovcara, you had the capacity and the ability to protect the cars; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We protected them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I would like clarification is this: You went to Ovcara on the 19th with Major Sljivancanin, and you told us that he had expressed concern about those cars. And I think it was him who suggested that they should be taken to Velepromet. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Am I right in saying it was his suggestion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when were the cars moved?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done by the centre for collection in Velepromet. I think that they were handed over on the 20th in the morning. A group of their people came from Velepromet. Ljubinko Stojanovic, the so-called TO chief, came with his people and transported all of the cars. All of the cars were transported to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And, therefore, by the end of the morning on the 20th of November, the likelihood of civilians coming to the Ovcara area unannounced was removed, wasn't it, because the cars had been taken to Velepromet. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our task was to remove the coarse. Now, as to the possibility of those people returning, I wasn't familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it means that civilians would not be coming to Ovcara on the afternoon of the 20th or the evening of the 20th, because the cars were no longer there. The risk was diminished, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken to Croatian, Mr. Moore, to Serbia. Do you understand that? So not a single person remained there. They were transported according to their wishes; some to Croatia, some to Serbia. So their return followed, I don't know, a month or two later, but there was no possibility of them returning on the following day to reclaim their cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you this question, you may or may not be able to help me with the answer. Do you know how it was that individuals knew that the Ovcara facility was empty on the afternoon of the 20th and the evening of the 20th? Do you know how that was ascertained?
