What I'm wondering is that somebody might have actually gone to Ovcara, and there were actually people in it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Because our understanding is that the Ovcara facility apparently was chosen in the afternoon of the 20th or the early hours of the afternoon of the 20th. That seems to be the impression.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your insistence on that topic is something that I am not familiar with. I'm telling you, I did not know about Ovcara at all. Don't ask me about that. Now, whether it was vacant, not vacant, who said what, I don't know. I have no answer for you concerning that, because I simply didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will move then on to a different topic. Let us deal with the 20th and the fact that you returned from Ovcara, and you went to what I will call the command post area at Negoslavci. Do you follow the topic I want to deal with?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When everything is clear, then I understand everything. Why don't you start and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will do my best. Your state of knowledge at that time when you returned to the command post was: There had been a selection process at the hospital with the Petrova Gora TO threatening, but nothing happening. Secondly, your state of knowledge was that at the JNA barracks, there had been quite severe threats and that you communicated that to Sljivancanin, but nothing had happened apart from, as you said, a few slaps. And the third element was you had been to Ovcara, and you had seen the same group, along with others, and clearly, acts of violence had been committed, obviously not on your individuals, but acts of violence had been committed, and there was an extremely hostile atmosphere at the time. Would that be a fair analysis of your state of knowledge vis-a-vis that topic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of that is true, as I described it. Up until Ovcara, yes, there were such manifestations. I was aware of them. It was conveyed to me, and all of that did exist to the extent that I described in my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You come to the command post. I think you told us in evidence, it was 4.00 or 4.30 in the afternoon. Can we just assume, rather than try and work out time, between light and dark; it might have been around dusk, would that be correct or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was still light. When I left Ovcara, it was still light. But within about half an hour, what we call winter dusk set on, and that usually happens between 4.00 and 4.30, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal with your decision to go and see your commander, Mr. Mrksic. You used the phrase, if my longhand note is correct: "My duty was to brief him of the changes and the problems at Ovcara." What do you mean by the phrase "my duty?"

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you what I mean by that phrase, well, that was my duty, my obligation, because the circumstances forced me in the situation where I found myself at Ovcara. So that entire trip from the barracks to Ovcara was not familiar to me, but I stayed there until the end. I could have abandoned it halfway through, but that would not have been proper. I had to perservere to the end and complete my task. And why did I have this need? Our books and our regulations stipulate that the commander is the most responsible person in an area of responsibility, so he is to be credited and to be blamed for everything. So just prior to the briefing, I went to inform him, because all of the commanders were supposed to be present at that point in time, and then he would be able to resolve the problem and issue a direct task to the commander of the 80th Brigade to undertake measures. That was my an assumption. Battalion commanders, brigade commander were all there; they were briefed about the problem. That was the best and the most opportune moment to resolve the problem. In that sense, I waited for half an hour or an hour, didn't leave right away. That was my duty, as an officer, given that there were problems, that the whole course of events had changed. I was duty-bound to say -- to report on what had happened, to ensure that it would not happen later on, so that measures could be taken to prevent the problem from escalating and to ensure that it was solved. To that end, I acted preventively in order to inform the commander, Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Bit it's right you had been told that the JNA barracks, when you went there, that the commander had ordered the buses to go to Ovcara. So on the information that you had available to you, you were aware that the commander himself had ordered that the buses go to Ovcara. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was stated; those were the statements. I didn't know. That was the information I received from a subordinate, Mr. Predojevic. So all of that is correct, yes. I heard that the commander had ordered to go to Ovcara, but it wasn't enough for me to conclude that it was normal. My impressions was that something was not logical, normal. I received the task and all of a sudden the task was changed. I couldn't disrupt the implementation of the task. The rule is that you complete the task and, then if you have reasons to complain to protest then you do that. But you don't abandon your task halfway through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you use the phrase "not normal," may I suggest the word that it was "odd" what had happened?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened where? Ovcara? Well, yes, it was odd. I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why was it odd?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the change of direction was odd to me. I didn't know why the direction was being changed. I had prepared myself and focused on the task. The barracks, and then from the barracks straight to Mitrovica. That was how I prepared myself. That was my basic task. And then at some point in time, you receive a different itinerary and you have no information concerning that. Nobody gives you the exact information. You just hear this person said that, this person said that; and then you arrived at the spot and then you realise that the situation is odd. Yes, odd is the right word. You said it right. Had it not been that way, it would not have been odd. Had they remained at the barracks, everything would have been all right. That's where the problem lies, but I was not part of the problem. I was simply executing my task. I would like for you to tell me who constituted the problem on the route between barracks and Ovcara. That's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I then deal with it this way. While it may have been odd, the information was that had been at the commander's order. So when you went to see the commander, would it be right to say that it was a two-fold purpose: One, to confirm that Mrksic had indeed been responsible for the redirection; and two, to let him know that there were events and incidents happening at both the barracks and, more particularly, Ovcara, that gave you cause for concern? Would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter one is correct. And as for the former one, it was not part of my confidence for me to go and double-check what the commander had ordered. He knows what he had ordered, and he's here so you can check with him. As for the latter, then, yes, if he is fully conscious of what he had ordered, then there is nothing for me to say. But perhaps he wasn't fully familiar or wasn't familiar at all with what had happened there. And in that case, I, as a direct executor of the task, then, yes, it was my role to inform him that there had been problems there, to inform him of the problems and to suggest measures. It is up to me to suggest measures. Now, as to whether the commander would accept my measures or define different measures on his own, that's his prerogative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you went, it was to inform him about the problems that caused you concern, and to try and ascertain if there were measures that could avoid those problems from escalating out of control; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, I think, said, "You may go." Consequently, is one to assume that he gave you no instructions about what to do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: He did not contact anybody in your presence to overcome the perceived problems; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. There was a meeting that he attended after that; in other words, there was a briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, listen to the question, please. He did not contact anybody in your presence to overcome the perceived problems. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: He did not explain to you about the government or the change of route. That is correct also, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it is also correct to say that he did not state or indicate to you that he had received instructions or guidance from other officers or senior officers. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on, then, dealing with Mr. Sljivancanin. The briefing was somewhere around 6.00ish. Obviously, it would tend to vary, but you saw Mr. Sljivancanin arrive for a brief moment; that is right, isn't it? You've given evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. He went to the commander's briefing; that is right, isn't it, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you had given this information to Mrksic prior to the commander's briefing; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then you spoke to Mr. Sljivancanin. Now, it's my -- my apologies for missing something. When you saw Sljivancanin and he was on his way to the commander's briefing, is it right you very briefly mentioned about the problems that you had seen that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Just in a couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. So when Mr. Sljivancanin came or you spoke to Mr. Sljivancanin, I think it is as a result of him summoning you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that you informed Mr. Sljivancanin, basically, of the same facts that you had told Colonel Mrksic? That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And as far as you are aware, he did not contact Mrksic about the information that you gave him.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, he did not pick up a telephone or he did not say, "I'm on my way to see Mrksic." That's all you can say, isn't it. He did not do anything like that; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was doing. At that time while I was with him, no. But I did not sit there for hours. We were there for half an hour and then I went on. I don't know if called him or not. While I was there, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well, we will deal the half hour while you were there. Through that half hour, he did not contact Mrksic. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: He, on your evidence, did not suggest to go to Ovcara to try and see if there were any problems that he could resolve. That is correct on your evidence that you have given.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't suggest anything to me. Now, as to whether he suggested anything to the commander or not, that's not something that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have asked a simple question. We're dealing with the 30 minutes. It is right to say within that 30-minute period when you gave him that same information that you had given Mrksic, on the evidence that you had given, he did not suggest going to Ovcara. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is also right to say that in your presence, he did not contact anyone to ascertain what was happening at Ovcara. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it is also correct to say that he said that he would probably look into it later.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And on the evidence that you have, and the knowledge that you have, you are not aware of him actually looking into it. This is on the evidence you have given.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment. I just want to try to clarify matters so I can speed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is slightly out of sequence in time, but I want to deal with this topic if I may. My apologies if I haven't got it quite word perfect. Is it right that you went into the hangar at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? On the day when I transported the people there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My apologies for being presumptuous. I'm talking about when the people were taken there on the 20th. Did you go into the hangar? Do you remember the three buses that you went, and you went and you saw Mr. Panic and you had a chat?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- on the 20th, when I saw Mr. Panic, I was in the hangar and I actually did something about those people. I threw them out. That's what I talked about. I said that I was there and that I threw these people out, if that is what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is what I am talking about. Thank you. You used the phrase in evidence - I've written it down longhand, so my apologies - "They are under our control. They are under our jurisdiction." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the word itself tells you what I meant. They are under the jurisdiction of the army, not of any other unit. The army was the sole party responsible at that time there, and that is why the army carried out the evacuation, carried out the whole operation. And now, at one point, all of a sudden, this is not something that belongs -- that is under our control. It is now somebody else there, and that is why I thought that we had an obligation to act here as part of the Operations Group South. So this was the sense in which I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A simple question: On the night of the 20th of November when those people were in the Ovcara hangar - and we know about the background. Not only from you, but from others - it is right to say, is it not, that once the police were withdrawn, those individuals in the hangar were completely unprotected? That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was not aware of that. But from this vantage point when we say that this is what happened, then, yes, that is what happened. But I was not aware of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am not discussing your personal circumstances. I am merely giving you a situation. You were privy to what was happening. I am asking you the simple question: That the once the police, the military police were withdrawn, those individuals in the hangar were completely unprotected. That is right, isn't it, from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is how it was, then yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So who issued the withdrawal of the military police on the evening of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I didn't know anything about that. And in fact, to this day, I don't know who ordered that, and I would like to know and I'm looking forward to learning that. That's the real answer, and this must be proven who ordered this to be done? I am waiting with great anticipation to learn that, and I would like to know who it was that ordered for this unit to stop securing the site and to leave the people there, the people for whom I had put my life on the line several times. And this is why I would like to urge you, Your Honours, to determine that. This is the crux of the matter. This is the most important thing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you really put your life on the line at the Ovcara hangar on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to apologise. It may seem strange to you here, but this is war that we're talking about. I can't really explain to you how often one risks one's life in war, unless you, yourself, fought in a war. And I have seen a lot of fighting, and this is how it is in the war. You risk your life all the time. I am not a trainee soldier, I'm not a rookie, I'm an experienced soldier. So I put my life on the line to protect these people, and this is really what I did. I'm not saying this to boast or anything. I just wanted to say that we officers in this unit of the OG South; that we were all honourable, honest people, that we abided by the Geneva Conventions and laws and customs of war, and there can be no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is that why you said to Mr. Sljivancanin that things could be so different in wartime circumstances when you were briefing him about the dangers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Please don't try to establish a link between what I said and this. I merely wanted to explain to you, in light of your allegations that I was responsible in some way for this. I merely wanted to say to you that I really made every effort I could to protect these people; anything that was within my purview as an officer, as a professional, as a person charged with completing a task. I merely said this as an aside, so you cannot really say this, what you just put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I can say it, because it's what your evidence is. It's at page 40, line 3. It was vis-a-vis and relation to the conversation you had with Sljivancanin. "I told him security was all right, but I also warned them that actions such as these might be a bit difficult under the circumstances that prevailed at the time in this wartime situation." So you are actually indicating that it was the prevailing circumstances at the time, being a wartime situation, that might make it even worse; isn't that right? Isn't that your point?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I merely wanted to let Major Sljivancanin know that these procedures, separating people in groups, releasing them; and then if this procedure were to be repeated, that this would irritate further people who were already quite irritated. And the best option was for people not to be in contact with them, for them to be isolated; and that would be the highest level of security one could provide them. So to prevent anyone from getting on the buses, into the hangar, so these people could be kept sort of untouchable. So while they were in transport, that actually opened up the possibility for these people to vent this aggressive behaviour. And that is why I suggested that this not be done any further, but that only the first -- that after the first group, no further groups be processed in this way. Isolation was the only solution, the only way in which they could have been saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. Your Honour, I have cut down my cross-examination, although it may not be immediately apparent, significantly. And I thought that I would run until the witching hour of a quarter to 1.00. I would like to move on to a different topic, and I would also like to pare down my cross-examination for this afternoon, which would mean that the next witness could start this afternoon, I would think, fairly easily. Could I possibly ask the Court's indulgence to rise a little early and perhaps resume a little early, if that's possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean now, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's exactly what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is early, perhaps, not a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there inconvenience for anybody of counsel or in the courtroom and those assisting if we resumed at a quarter to 2.00 rather than 2.00? I'm trying to see through clouded glass. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to make a point in advance. It might happen with our next witness, and I will know more about that during the break, for him to start later, because from what I know now, Mr. Maric was interviewed by Mr. Weiner, from the Prosecution. This is what we scheduled yesterday, and I wanted Mr. Bulatovic to be present and Mr. Weiner said that he would agree. And if it is indeed the case if Mr. Bulatovic told me that he had been told about it and that he attended the interview, that there would be no need for any further proofing of Witness Maric, then we will agree to Mr. Moore ending sooner and I will not have too much of a re-examination,. But if we learn that the witness has already been proofed or that it was done not in the presence of Mr. Bulatovic, then I might ask for a little postponement. So this is a little caveat here, but I will be able to let you know after the break what the situation is. And I just wanted to take this opportunity, after the end of Mr. Vukasinovic's testimony, I wanted to inform you about our plan, how we plan to proceed with our case. I think it would be quite useful for us to acquaint you with the development of our case. I think that we are set to end our case, perhaps even sooner than the deadline. I think it would be good to tell you that in light of the return of P002 to the courtroom, but I will be able to tell you more about that after Mr. Vukasinovic is excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we will be in suspense all over the lunch break. You realise we're sitting longer hours at the moment to finish within the time you've indicated, and I wanted to ensure that counsel were conscious of this so we were making most use of the available time. So we look forward to what you have to say and I have not detected any problem about a quarter to 2.00 start so we will adjourn now and resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.25 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, I want to go on to the -- you've given us one account of your evidence. I want to deal with the other account because you unusually give two accounts. I want you to turn, please, to the statement of the Office of the Prosecutor which is, in your case, tab 6, in the English, tab 5. You've already seen it because Mr. Vasic referred to it. Now, as I say, it's tab 6 for you, and I've had all the paragraphs individually numbered to help. Have you got it there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have two short questions before we commence. You told us, I think, that you were born in Kosovo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why do you give your ethnic origin as Montenegrin?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because my father is a Montenegrin from Montenegro, and I am entitled to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You are entitled to put wherever you want, Mr. Vukasinovic, even Khazakstan. But as far as I am concerned, I just wanted to know why Montenegro. The second question is simply this: Names of the persons present during the interview, I see you've got Mr. Borisavljevic present with you. Is that right or not? Was he present at some time the interview, as is being suggested?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean, that he was present where? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the front page, it gives your name, family name; it gives your first name; it gives your date of birth, 15th of August, 1954. So you are about a year and three months younger than Mr. Sljivancanin; and then right down at the bottom, "Names of all persons present during interview." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that. I have to apologise. Now I do know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So we've got Mr. Borisavljevic, Dzuro, Paolo Pastore-Stocchi, Franjic; and then a gentleman, I presume, from the commission of cooperation with The Hague. Now, merely inquiring, Mr. Borisavljevic, is that the same Borisavljevic who was a member of the security organ with responsibility, in a neutral sense, for Velepromet in 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was the date of interview was the 16th and the 26th of November. I presume that the interview was on the 16th, and then there was, I presume again, a rereading; is that right? Can you just help us on that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Mr. Borisavljevic, was he there during the interview? You see sometimes --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Mr. Vladimir Dzuro conducted the interview in the presence of Paolo, the interpreter, and there was also Colonel Mojsilovic and myself. So that is a mistake. If that's what it says here, then that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, was Borisavljevic with you on one of these days, even if he wasn't there during the interview?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So we can just disregard how Mr. Borisavljevic's name got there. We can just put a pen through it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, you can just go ahead and do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So there is no misunderstanding, I have made inquiries of whether he was there or not; and from the OTP position, they can't remember. And you say he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I say now that he was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we deal then with certain aspects of your OTP statement; page or paragraph 13, which is 4 of 10 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Paragraph 13, and I have no doubt at all that you have read this statement recently, haven't you? Yes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Paragraph 13 reference to: "I know that in mid-November, 1991, shortly before the fall of Vukovar, Seselj visited our zone of operation." Now, we have heard evidence that Seselj apparently visited on the 13th of November, which clearly is shortly before the fall of Vukovar. Would that date or interval be consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was a bit earlier than that. As far as I can recall, it was earlier than that. I can't give you an exact date. I think it was actually before the 13th. I can't recall the date; I only know that it was in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you asked by Mr. Lukic about the Seselj visit when you were being proofed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just look, then, at what is said in paragraph 13. You have personally nothing to do with this visit. "I know for a fact he visited members of the Serbian Radical Party in Vukovar, as his volunteers were within our military composition when he was visiting those units. He also visited the area of our responsibility. And then I know that many members of the Leva Supoderica were volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party," and then you go on to say how he arrived, and that you saw him pass the command post in Negoslavci. It's the next line that I want to deal with if I may. "I also know for a fact that he visited the command of the TO of Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica. Those command posts were located in private houses in the area of Petrova Gora." Now, "I also know for a fact that he visited," how do you know for a fact that he visited? Was it a case that, perhaps, you were at that meeting, in the most honest of reasons, of course?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at the meeting. But I do know that he was visiting the forward area; and, quite naturally, he came to see them. He specifically arrived there to see them, not us. But I was not at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it goes on: "It would be natural that somebody from the security organs of the Guards Brigade monitored this visit. It was the responsibility of Captain Borce Karanfilov, because he was the security officer assigned to the 1st Assault Detachment. But I do not know if he was present at this meeting, and I know that Seselj's visit lasted one day." Well, now, you saw Seselj arrive. You said here in your statement that it would be logical and sensible for the security organ to be present or -- I beg your pardon, to monitor the visit. Did you inquire from anyone whether they had been to that Seselj visit at Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not within my purview to investigate, but I know that when I was the commander of the command post, that this visit occurred. He went to the command post. He couldn't have gotten in without my knowing that. I know that he went to the combat positions in order to visit his volunteer units. But when you ask me whether it would be normal, it would be normal for somebody to monitor that, and that's what I was asked by the investigator. That's what I said. It would be normal to monitor it, but not in such a way that you are actually sitting there all the time. But you have to get intelligence data about the visit and see what the purpose of it was. That's normal. So at the time, Borce Karanfilov was in charge of that unit because it was a peacetime unit. I don't know whether he was there. That's what I stated, and I can't tell you whether he attended it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think there may be an objection with Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, the interpreters are to blame this time. Page 64, line 23, and the witness said, "When asked by the investigator whether that would be normal, this was the response that he gave."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not quite sure what that means, but the reality is that it's a statement that you signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. You had been in the Vukovar area for how long?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 30th of September until the 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you ever aware of Seselj coming on previous occasions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Because he was a fairly high-profile political figure, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know how he was able to make his way to the houses that were located in the area of Petrova Gora? Do you know what assistance he got for guidance to get there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had his own security, his bodyguards, his fighters that escorted him, so he had his own security detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to look at paragraph 17 of this statement. It's at the very bottom of that paragraph. It relates to the Velepromet facility. "I believe that most of those people in this collection centre were civilians. I do not know about any mistreatment that would take place in this centre, but I believe that Captain First Class Borisavljevic would be able to provide for detailed information about what was going on there. I only went there once or twice." Now, you had the name of Borisavljevic at the start of your witness statement, it must have been an error. Do you know Mr. Borisavljevic? Do you still know him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him. He was my colleague. We worked together. He is retired now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know, and I don't want the exact address, but are you in contact with him? If need be, can he be contacted?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he can be contacted. I have not been in touch with him recently. He has some health problems, but he can be contacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if the Defence wanted to contact him and call him as a witness, you would be willing and able to assist them, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If need be, absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we just move on. Page 6 of 10, paragraph 25. I want to ask you about one or two issues in this paragraph. I read as follows: "Due to my recognised natural authority, I was tasked by Major Sljivancanin with preventing any violent incidents around the hospital. I personally talked to Miroljub Vujovic and Stanko Vujanovic. I told Miroljub Vujovic that he should keep men under control. One of those fighters pointed a rifle to my stomach and threatened to kill me. I remember that we had a nasty argument there." Now, may I deal with one or two parts of that statement. "Due to my recognised natural authority," - perhaps I'm guilty more of curiosity than anything else - but what is "recognised natural authority?" How does one demonstrate that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's up to those who work with me to explain it to you. Now I have to tell you about myself; is that right? Okay. Well, you can ask my superior officers. I was -- I was not easily frightened. I was reliable. I was responsible and persistent, and that is all very important. This is what -- this is what you have to demonstrate, because if you don't, then the other side will win. So this is the state of mind, the spirit that you have to show to those people; because then, they cannot make any wilful decisions. They have to abide by what is asked of them. So this is the essence of my natural authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "One of those fighters pointed a rifle to my stomach and threatened to kill me." Where did that occur? Was that at the barracks or was that at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened both at the barracks and in the hospital. At the barracks, it was when I was taking the people out; and in the hospital, it was just across the road when I went there to talk to them, when the major had released the people that we had brought back and one of them asked me: "What are you doing?" And he was holding his rifle trained at me and -- well, that incident then ended and -- so these are all the situations in which, if you show fear, you lose the battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So just so we get it accurately, one of them was the Petrova Gora group of people who put a gun in your stomach; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you said it also happened at the barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. And also at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you had guns pulled on you personally on at least three occasions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably even more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we move to paragraph 27, because I want to look at this in comparison with the evidence that you have given. "I took the first group of prisoners of war out of the hospital before the argument between Sljivancanin and Borsinger. A representative of the ICRC took place on the bridge over the river in Vukovar. I do not know why Major Sljivancanin did not allow Red Cross representatives to come to the hospital, but I know that all those selected people were transported out of the hospital before the Red Cross was allowed in." Now, I have asked you questions earlier on about whether the ICRC and the ECMM were present or not when you returned. You suggested that they were there when you returned. But on this particular paragraph, there is a clear statement which suggests the contrary. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. When you look at this answer, that's how it was, but the question that the investigator asked me was completely different from the one that you're now asking me. He asked me, "Did you see representatives of the Red Cross there when you were pulling the second group out?" And I said, "No, because I didn't see them." I said that I had seen journalists, reporters, when they were at the hospital. But as for the first question, my answer was like this because I didn't know why Major Sljivancanin had not allowed them to cross the bridge. This is something that I just didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it's not that part - I can certainly deal with it if you wish - but it's not that part that I'm asking. I'm asking how it is you say, "Two hours or one hour ago, half of the evacuees were taken to the barracks, you then returned. I returned," I think it was around about 10.30, somewhere around about there. And you remained for approximately two and a half hours when the ICRC and the ECMM were supposed to be there. Here, in plain language, it says that in actual fact: "They were transported out of the hospital." All - note the word, "all those selected people were transported out of the hospital before the Red Cross was allowed in." Now, I'm suggesting to you that sentence indicates perfectly clearly that you knew that they were all out before the ICRC came in, doesn't it? And it is completely contradictory to what your evidence was an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know this thing that you're claiming now. I said that the representatives of the International Red Cross had been in the hospital. I did not say that they were there next to the persons that had been separated. I -- that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will move on.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this sense, I said that they had not been there. It's -- it seems that you don't understand what I'm saying, and I don't understand what you're saying. I'm telling you about one single spot there on the site, and you are now talking about this entire situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I wanted to move off. I'll come back and deal with this. Let us look what it says: "I took the first group of prisoners of war out of the hospital before the argument between Sljivancanin and Borsinger. A representative of the ICRC took place on the bridge over the Vuka river in Vukovar." Now we know that was around about 10.00. "I do not know why Sljivancanin did not allow the Red Cross representative to come to the hospital, but I know that all those selected people were transported out of the hospital before the Red Cross was allowed in." Now, I don't hear any change in the translation with regard to this particular matter. So, how do you reconcile that perfectly clean statement and the evidence that you gave at about 12.15?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reiterate my original statement, that they were in the hospital, but not on the spot where I was taking the people that I was tasked with transporting. In that sense, I gave this statement. I didn't give a statement that they were not in the hospital, as a whole. This refers particularly to the group that I was transporting out of it, but it does say so here, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is all the questions I wish to ask you about that statement. There are many more, but I will cut down the time. Finally, and there are a lot of other statements, but I want to deal with English tab 7, B/C/S tab 8. It relates to an interview at Novi Sad on the 28th of November, 2003. Now, have you got that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just go through one or two parts. The first B/C/S page -- there is a mandatory warning, but the first B/C/S page that I want to deal with is English page 2, B/C/S page 0346-5363, and it would be approximately halfway down the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want you to confirm one part of the evidence on this. You said that: "I saw many people there," this is clearly Ovcara, "when I got closer. I saw Lieutenant-Colonel Panic. He did not go inside. When I went in, I saw that many prisoners were covered in blood and beaten up." It's page 4 of the English version. Do you agree with that statement as being an accurate record of what you saw?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us then go to page 0346-5364. English page 5. This is the account that I suggest you have not put before this Bench. It reads: "At one point that afternoon ..." Have you got that? It's at the top of the page, second paragraph. "At one point that afternoon, sometime around 1700 hours ..." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "At one point that afternoon sometime around 1700 hours, I informed Colonel Mrksic that the situation there had been critical and that I had brought it under control. I also pointed out that those men had remained there. The colonel did not comment at all, and he did not say that anything further should be done." Now, it's the next part I want to deal with. "Major Sljivancanin was not at Ovcara that day at all. When he returned to the command post sometime around 2130 hours and asked me to go with him to Ovcara because he had heard there had been problems there, so we went there together. When we got there, the police captain on duty reported to Sljivancanin and did not mention any problems." So do you confirm that that is, again, the fourth time that you have indicated that you went with Sljivancanin to investigate troubles at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could we deal, then, please, with that same page 5364, and I think it's about three-fifths down the page in B/C/S version. It's page 6 in the English, halfway down the English page. It reads: "I said that the hospital had been evacuated on the 19th of November." Have you got that part?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "And that I was at Ovcara on the 19th of November. On the 20th of November, I did not go to Ovcara." Now, the next is the part I wish to deal with: "I knew Stanko, Miroljub, and Kameni only by sight. I did not speak to them that day at all. Sljivancanin knew them better as he had more frequent contacts with them." So do you agree that Sljivancanin knew them better because he had more frequent contacts with them? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What contacts did he have with them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll have to ask him that. I don't know. I cannot answer on behalf of Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You can answer on the basis of what you have seen and what you have been told. That's perfectly permissible. So, if you agree that that is accurate, what is the basis for the statement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not understand you. You ask of me something which is outside my powers, but I will try to answer. These are virtual questions. I've never been asked such questions. So we have combat operations carried out. People come and go. It is known who are the commanders, and now you ask me how we knew them. Of course, we had to have contacts with them, because we subsumed them into our combat establishment and formations; and most probably he saw them there when he was on that spot. This is most probably that this is the kind of contact that he had. You think that we sat down together and ate and drank every day. But you know, in war, 15 or 20 days may pass without seeing somebody. It is quite unnatural for me to explain how a third person knows somebody else. If you want to ask me about my contacts, I can tell you. If you want to hear from Mr. Sljivancanin about his contacts, you should ask him. What I know is that they had contacts during the touring of units and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The English translation used the word, "they were you subsumed within ours." Subsumed normally in English means "included within." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Borovic please keep his voice down?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the answer first, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Representatives of those volunteer -- I mean, Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora units, these fighters were under the command of our 1st Assault Detachment, and they fought within our units, in the composition of our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal -- sorry, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to this answer, now it is clear. But the witness, prompted by the Prosecutor, did not say that they were included in our units. They were included in the combat establishment or deployment of our units. But since the witness answered in the correct way, now my objection has no grounds. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to deal with a document which I believe was published on the (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: (redacted) Shall I just pass it forward to you, and English translations for the Court. May I just pass this forward?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, as I've said, you know that you have referred specifically to one person in this article. Please, we will both try not to mention that person's name. Do you follow me? We will just call him "the witness." So can we just deal then, please, with the article itself. "Dear readers and journalists in particular, I believe that there is not a single fairly literate person in this country who has not in their youth enjoyed reading about spectacular adventures of the king of all liars. Baron Munchausen including among other things about his flying on a cannon ball. Obviously, the baron inspired many a young generation. Only the modern big-time liars fly by planes and land in The Hague, and then in front of TV cameras. And an audience dressed in black robes and white bibs, they take part in the show supposedly called a trial. The greatest irony is that this show has been staged for the purpose of establishing the truth." I won't ask you any questions about individuals dressed in black robes and white bibs, so you can relax in relation to that. Let us move to the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "Since," and which refer to the witness "took part in this farce of planetary proportions as a witness, who devoted most of his time reminiscing about Vukovar and the events which I personally was involved, and since the only truth about these events is that they are a blatant lie..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've got versions for the interpreters. Your Honour, I've got versions for the interpreters. I thought they had been given, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would be useful if they could be passed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may suggest that we go into private session because Mr. Moore just stated the date, the hour, the name of the paper and the byline of the author. I do believe that this may be helpful if publicised to pinpoint the witness, because there is an archive of all newspapers. It is not my witness, but I do believe that this would be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm quite happy to go into private session if there is a risk. I don't think it was identifiable as my learned friends, but it may become that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was obviously Mr. Moore's opinion, not a question. I think that he was not trying to elicit any response, and I think that this is not a proper way to complete the cross-examination, and as regards this document. I would like to be allowed to conduct my redirect and then perhaps that would be the right moment to decide. So I would first present my views on this document and through my redirect, and then we can decide on that ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the last part of the intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There was some words of yours at the end that were lost, Mr. Lukic. Are they worth repeating?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I'm not opposed to an MFI being given to this document, but I just wanted to ask you, first, to be allowed to ask some questions in redirect about this document, and then to give you my views about the admission of this document into evidence. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear your re-examination, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us begin with this document, this article published in the newspaper. Mr. Vukasinovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I must interrupt you. I think we both knew from all the signals of counsel that Mr. Moore had finished his cross-examination, but the record doesn't reveal it. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The signals were right, but I didn't utter the words, I'm sorry. That concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I didn't want you to have a false start, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I criticise my colleague, Mr. Moore, before I begin my re-examination. I have noticed that he is in the habit of concluding his cross-examination by making comments rather than questions. But I have to admit that this time, he really, in my opinion, went too far. But let us now try to complete this witness's evidence in a more appropriate manner and more normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, this article that we've been talking about, is this a response to an article by this person?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. In order for this to be reliable, you would have to find the initial article for Mr. Moore, and then you could get a proper idea of what this was all about. But you're using just the part that you wanted and you needed.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) This was the darkest possible account that could have been published. That was what was done by this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will go on, but, sir, can you please just give me very brief answers. Is this text a response to some facts that were published about your unit, your colleagues in the course of Vukovar operation, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The facts that Mr. Moore asked you about, are they presented here in response to the facts that were claimed as such by this man?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this man, as far as you know, or has this man ever contacted you and your colleagues to ask you about facts that pertain to the events in Vukovar, to interview you, to talk to you? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He's never contacted us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you the same question that me learned colleague, Mr. Borovic, did regarding the facts. Were you ever at the command post of Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. And I don't know how many times I have to repeat that. I never was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, as you say, this article is an emotional response on your part, to the way he presented the facts about your unit in his articles?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I will move on to some other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps you can now hear my views about this MFI. I oppose its admission into evidence because I think that it has no value, no weight. This is a document that speaks to the personality of a certain person, and this is a response to a text that we have not seen. We cannot compare it with anything. I think that this document is inadmissible, and its evidentiary value is quite small as to the facts. Now, as to the credibility, I think that the Trial Chamber has been able to satisfy itself about the credibility of this witness, and this document is not necessary for this purpose. It has absolutely no evidentiary weight with regard to proving the counts in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that the end of your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I have a few more questions, but I simply wanted to deal with this issue, but perhaps it would be good for me to complete my redirect and then we can release the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would be good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, I will first ask you a few questions regarding Mr. Vasic, in fact, Mr. Vasic's examination, and we both have to slow down. I have to apologise to the interpreters. Now, please look at your statement under tab 6. Now I want you to focus on paragraph 16 that Mr. Vasic referred to. And he read to you that you said, among other things, "Our tasks included," meaning the Guards Brigade's tasks, "the evacuation of POWs and civilians from Vukovar." That's what you said. Now, my question to you is who escorted the prisoners of war from Vukovar when they were being evacuated? Which unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there is an error in interpretation. Page 91, line 13, these are the evacuations as tasks and here the term is in singular, the evacuation, and my colleague can confirm whether this is indeed the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The whole sentence reads as follows: "Security organs in the Guards Brigade had regular tasking throughout the combat activities. Among other things, our tasks included evacuation of prisoners of war." This is in singular but obviously this means plural, "evacuations."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So my question to you is which unit escorted the prisoners of war, because this is the term used in this statement, from Vukovar, when they left?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a unit from the 1st Battalion of the military police, the 1st Company of the military police with armed personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. No, in general, what kind of unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who secured the prisoners of war while they were in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security of prisoners of war was in the purview of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of those transports in which the prisoners of war were evacuated; for instance, the Mitnica transport, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commanding officer of the military police, so the one who was directly in command of the unit in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the officers in the military police units, who were they subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Guards Brigade, the military police units, two battalions, were directly subordinate to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic asked you - that's page 69 of the draft version of the transcript. You don't have that here. That's the transcript of the proceedings - and you said regarding your contacts with Captain Predojevic, you said that Captain Predojevic was in charge of the security of the barracks. That's what you said. Can a security organ issue an order to a commanding officer of the military police?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He cannot issue direct orders. But if authorised to do so by the brigade commander, he can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This discussion that you had with Predojevic, was it in the nature of issuing orders, or was its nature different? I'm referring to the conversation in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conversation with him did not contain any orders. This was not the tone. There was just the demand that measures be taken. In light of the situation, I simply asked him. I didn't order him. I asked him to take measures because this was something that he was authorised to do. So it was a request of the kind that one colleague makes to another colleague, because the security organs had a gentler approach to the chain of command issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic also read out to you a brief sentence from your testimony before the Belgrade court. That was at page 50. Can you please look at it, that's tab 10, page 50. That was the last question that he asked you. And that's where you said: "After a brief rest, I had lunch. I went to the command. It was sometime around 5.00, 5.30. I went to see whether Sljivancanin was there and to simply brief him, to see what the story was, why the people were there, and tell him what the situation was. I arrived there to the operations room, the colonel, or rather, the then Major Sljivancanin was not there. The commander was there." And then you describe -- well, we heard the account here in court, so I don't have to go into that. So my question to you is - and I think that you actually said that yesterday - where was physically the building where Mr. Sljivancanin's command post was? Was it in the same building or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about ten to 15 metres away from the OG South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So now my question to you is: Did you go to his command or to the OG South headquarters when this was going on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the OG South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had you wanted to see Sljivancanin himself, where would you have gone?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have gone to the building where his section was located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness replied already, so it's not relevant anymore. I think that the witness has already stated here. It is stated here who he wanted to see and where, so I think that this was a leading question. But now that the reply has already been given, this is really not relevant anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would just indicate that as it is when there are differences between the Prosecution and the Defence, so it should also be when there are differences being between Defence counsel, and we will follow the same pattern. If Mr. Lukic asks a question that is not obviously objectionable, I would think we should let the witness give his reaction to that before another counsel seeks to raise some point in objection. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we seem to be in a sort of situation where Defence starts objecting to a Defence's claims, but I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is a position where there is difference between the cases of different accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But the point is the witness is not a witness who is overwrought or overborne by what is happening here. The witness knows what is on his mind and speaks it very clearly. He can understand what is put to him; he can react. That reaction is more important and valuable to this Chamber than to have a counsel interject and to put their version on it and then to find the witness then speaks in similar words to the interjecting counsel. We are left thinking probably the answer was suggested to the witness; whereas, it may have been just what the witness wanted to say in the first place. So we get much more and learn much more about the witness's understanding if we hear his answer to questions which, on their face, are not objectionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand, and this is why, when Mr. Moore started asking his questions, I did not want to put forth such an objection. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, we are going to broach another subject. Mr. Moore, today and yesterday, repeatedly confronted you with your statements given at earlier times to different bodies and trying to pinpoint inconsistencies between your today's testimony and those statements, particularly in view of the fact and pertaining to your going to Ovcara with Mr. Sljivancanin on the 19th in the evening, or the 20th in the evening. In all your statements that you were confronted with by Mr. Moore to the security department in 1998, one month later before the military court, a statement to the OTP, a statement at Novi Sad. We're dealing with four statements then. Did any of your interviewers show you any documents, orders, decisions, anything dating from that relevant period?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, before going to be interviewed by these interviewers, did you have occasion to refresh your memory as to the dates of certain events by consulting your personal diary or maybe official notebook?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I did not have any such notebooks. We left them within our units when we left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you given an opportunity, after giving such statements, to consult any of the documents from the period?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which documents?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war log of the Guards Brigade, which helped me a great deal to recollect certain events that I had forgotten in the meantime, in talks with my colleagues and officers, superiors, where we discussed things to try to remember what happened when, because we had forgotten many things. And later, by seeing the statements, the documents, and some other documents that you showed me, and that I was confronted with from brigade commander's orders, documents from the superior command, et cetera, et cetera, everything has influenced an improvement in establishing in chronological order. Those events followed one another. There was certain lacunas. It was very difficult for me to tell two events apart. Sometimes, it all seems to have happened in a single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you use the war log for in terms of refreshing your memory? To which events did it pertain?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe this is something that Mr. Moore cannot understand. That I was convinced that the evacuation took place on the 19th. That on the 17th, we captured Vukovar. This is what I wrote. In my view, Vukovar was liberated on the 17th. This is what I remembered. But in the war log, I noticed that on the 19th, there was the visit of Cyrus Vance, and then I remembered then that day was not the day of the evacuation, but the following day. So -- because I had some obligations concerning Cyrus Vance's visit and that I had some other duties, that people from the security department had come there, and I remembered some other activities, then that the convoy from Croatia was returned to Ovcara. All these events that I could see recorded in that war log and which made me realise that my memory of these events was lacking accuracy. Eventually, I saw the date when commander departed for Belgrade. It was said 21st of November, 8.15, the commanding officer with some other officers departed for Belgrade. It stated so in the log.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While giving your first four statements before the Belgrade trials, so when you gave those statements and testimony of -- about which you were not questioned and I'm not going to question you either, did any of your interviewers state that they had some documents that they may show to you to jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any of your statements that we analysed today contain any of your interviewer's questions or do they contain only and solely your answers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, statements are composed of both questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we've reached the time for a break. I do believe that I have some five minutes more worth of questions, but if the time is right, maybe we can break now. Your Honours lead me please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We detect, in your voice, a plea and we will adjourn now and resume at quarter to -- I'm sorry, it must be half an hour. We've had redactions. Five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a handful of questions on one single topic, Mr. Vukasinovic, and this refers to Mr. Moore's question during his cross today. He asked you whether you knew anything about Sljivancanin allegedly doing something after the conversation you had on the 20th, after you had briefed him on the situation at Ovcara. My question is: On that day, did you attend the meeting of the OG South command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Responding to my question during my examination-in-chief, referring to your conversation with Sljivancanin. And I'm referring to page 52: "As far as I can remember, he was late in the briefing." [In English] "By my command post, We saw each other for a couple of seconds. I told him that I'd been at Ovcara and he was in passing. He said: I'm late, going to the briefing." [Interpretation] Is it known to you whether at meetings of the OG South command, since that you did not that day, but usually would Lieutenant-Colonel Panic attend such meetings of the OG South command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it known to you whether Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic would attend meetings at the OG South command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it known to you that Colonel Lesanovic and Gluscevic would attend OG South command meetings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is Major Sljivancanin obliged to inform you about conversations he had with Colonel Mrksic and when he conducted such conversations with Mr. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. There remains the motion of Mr. Moore for the admission of the article from the publication of Glas. We've heard submissions. In the Chamber's view, the article should be admitted under seal. Some elements of it may bear upon the credit we attach to the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will be admitted as Exhibit 860 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vukasinovic, you will be pleased to know that that concludes your evidence before the Tribunal. There will be no further questions for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here, and for the assistance that you have given us. And you are now, of course, free to return to your ordinary activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The court officer will show you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you rise for a reason, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I usually do not rise without reason. I would like to advise you about our further plans for the proceedings; but before doing so, I, by your leave, will have to say something. During these proceedings, we tried, under your guidance, to be observant, fair, and cultured. But Mr. Moore's address at the end of his cross-examination has translated into our language were: "You are a first-rate scoundrel." The word "scoundrel" in our language is very offensive. Maybe the term scoundrel in English is not as offensive, but my learned colleagues and I believe that a line has been overstepped. On several occasions during our examination, we've been advised not to impinge on a witness's integrity. But I believe that the comment, which was not a question by Mr. Moore, is something that no witness should really tolerate. And in the B/C/S, the word "nitkov," scoundrel is very offensive. What I'd like to brief you on as soon as possible is what we see as the state of play, so that we can impart what can be expected and we can prime ourselves for what is next. And we would like to hear from you guidance on further steps in these proceedings. Upon conversations with Mr. Sljivancanin and other consultations, we decided to give up certain witnesses which are repetitive, which would provide testimony on matters that have been testified to extensively. So our schedule for the forthcoming period would be as follows: We have two witnesses who are ready; one of them to start witness immediately, and the other maybe tomorrow or on Friday. Mr. Maric, who is in the court building, and Mr. Stojic, Petar, let me remind you, he is to testify about the visit of Mr. Vance, and I believe that we can deal with him within one working day. Next weekend, we expect the arrival of two witnesses to witness next week and they should be testifying for a longer period of time. The first of them is Mr. Karanfilov, and then Mladen Karan. As per our schedule and our assessment, each should take two days. So this may do away with the whole week next week. I believe that this is a realistic assessment, given all the parties in the proceedings. The next witness after those two who may take the stand as early as Friday next or failing that, on Monday, should be Susnjar Pero; and according to our estimates, he is going to testify to the events in the hospital on the 20th. He was there on behalf of the ICRC, and he may testify to other things that may known to him and he should take one day. Then we should like to summon our expert witness, Vuka Petar, who should take at most two days. And I believe that one session would be used per Defence and then he would be left for cross-examination. Which means that the other witnesses that we've listed; one Radakovic Dragan is inaccessible. I haven't been able to locate him. I heard that I was in Italy, but there's been no contact him. And other witnesses in, in our view, would be repetitive. And given your guidance to focus on the meritorious points and to which we may provide new facts, then we, given all that, we've abandoned some of our witnesses. So we've abandoned their viva voce testimony. So maybe the last two days of the week of December would be free.
