I believe that our assessment has been realistic, and I believe that those two free days would be ideal for the re-examination of Witness 002 to round off this stage in the proceedings. What will happen next is a point of conjecture. I believe that you should know that; and on the basis of that, you should provide guidance. Another thing, on behalf of all of the Defence teams, we have very grave difficulties with air transportation during the Christmas season. It would be very useful for us to know at least two or three days in advance what the plans would be so that we can plan our recess, our holidays, if there would be a recess. And I believe that we can make use of next week to deal with the proposals coming from Mr. Moore. I believe that it would be useful for everybody in this courtroom, primarily the Bench, to be guided by what we've explained now. We will seek tolerancy for we may be missed by one day, but I believe that we should be through by 7th of December. As far as Witness Maric, he is here and ready. Mr. Moore proposes that we start examination now. I was told that there is no audio tape of today's interview. It is up to you to discuss -- to decide whether we should start with Mr. Maric today or if we -- even if we were to start tomorrow, we will be finished with him within one and a half days. Of course it's not up to me to take this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would Your Honour just hear me on one matter before Your Honour makes any decision. It's in relation to Mr. Maric. Mr. Bulatovic has been present throughout the interview with the Office of the Prosecutor. The Defence are in no way unaware of what was said, and we would wish to start today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Maybe the interpretation was not correct. It is true, Mr. Bulatovic was at the interview. He heard it. But I said that the other Defence teams were not given the audiotape pertaining to Mr. Mr. Vasic. As far as the others are concerned, we are ready to conduct our examination immediately. This is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is incumbent upon me to rise, since I have been quoted by my colleague. We haven't been given either the proofing notes nor the audio tape of today's interview. The only thing I know is that he mentioned my client, and that he was the topic of conversation between the OTP and the witness. And at any rate, I should have this audio tape before examining the said witness, so that I may prepare my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, are you able to indicate when that will be available?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I have told Mr. Vasic before you came into court that that audio tape is being done, being miffed I think is the phrase, and it will be available to him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, can I just be clear. Looking at your amended 65 ter list, you are not planning now to call two further witnesses, is that correct, number 7 on the list and number 9 on the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. We are not going to call them, including the witnesses that are also referred to. I can tell you that number 19, 18, Witness 17, 15, and the two that you referred to will not be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That resolves those issues. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one small matter. Could I deal with it in chambers? It will take no time at all; but in fairness, it should be dealt with in chambers, if Your Honour could trust me to that extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When would you propose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Not in chambers, I beg your pardon, in closed session. Sorry, I'm a diehard.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the submissions you put earlier about the future programme, there was ventured the possibility of rebuttal witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate - and we don't press you if that's not yet clear - are you able to indicate whether there's any certainty about that matter yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is a matter which is actually being investigated today where we will know more specifically whether it is feasible or not, and I will have the answer tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Moore. We're grateful, Mr. Lukic, for the indications that you have given. The present programme, it would appear, could continue unchanged. And it may be if things go well, that you will finish a day or two days earlier than the programme allows, given the witnesses that are not to be called. We would indicate the Chamber's view that the witness being recalled, Witness P22, should be available for recall at the end of the case of Mr. Sljivancanin, and that may be the Thursday or the Friday of what had been the planned last week of Mr. Sljivancanin's evidence. If everything goes well, we may be able to finish then that evidence by the weekend. I'm searching for the precise date. I think the 8th of December was the Friday. It may be possible to conclude the definitely-known evidence by that time, but we must leave, for the moment, open the prospect of rebuttal evidence and that will remain on the four days that were previously indicated in mid-January, a Friday, Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday. The remainder of the time table for written submissions and oral submissions will remain as indicated. That being so, I think we should start on the witness. It will fortunately be possible overnight for Mr. Vasic and Mr. Borovic to have the tape, it appears. And it may be that we'll be able to continue with that evidence without interruption. But if that's not possible, interruption will have to occur. So if the witness could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read allowed the affirmation on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Bulatovic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Before we start with your examination, I would like to give you some guidance in order for everything we say to be transposed accurately into the record. Please listen to my question and then start your answer after I finish so that we don't overlap, because that causes problems for the interpreters. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, could you please state your full name for the record, your date of birth, your father's name.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: My name is Mladen Maric. My father's name was Bogdan. And I was born on the 21st of September in 1960 in Novi Travnik, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Since 1975 until 1979, according to the information I was given by you, you attended the military high school in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And then from 1979 until 1983, you attended the military academy of the ground forces infantry?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1983, you were the commander of the 1st Platoon of the military police, 2nd Military Police company, Military Police Battalion in the Motorised Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was not the commandant but kommandir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1984, you were a lieutenant, and you had completed a course for the military police officers in Parace; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And then you became the commander of the 2nd Military Police Company in the 2nd Military Police Battalion in the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1987, you had the rank of captain and then you received the rank of a major later on?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1990, you became a member of the anti-terrorist military police company that was part of the 1st Military Police Battalion of the Motorised Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, you were promoted to the rank of Captain First Class; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 [Realtime transrcript read in error "1992"], you were appointed to the post of the deputy commander of the 1st Military Police Battalion of the Motorised Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says 1991 in the transcript, it should read 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, you were promoted to the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1996, you left the army, were no longer an active dutyman?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, after those preliminary data, your curriculum vitae, I would like us to turn to the events in Vukovar and the time when your company was dispatched to Vukovar. Can you please tell us when that happened, how was your company dispatched there, and what was its composition at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: The company was dispatched in late September. I think it was on the 30th of September as part of the Motorised Guards Brigade or the battalion that we belonged to. We were sent to the Vukovar sector, and an element of our company was deployed in combat on the 2nd of October. You also asked me about the composition of our company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the composition of the company.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: The anti-terrorist company --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak a little bit slower for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: The anti-terrorist military police company had its command element. The first platoon of the military police, these were officers, and two platoons of the military police composed of soldiers, rank and file soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who were the komandiri of the platoons?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: The komandir of the 1st platoon was (redacted). The second platoon was commanded by Lieutenant Zeljko Bajic. The commander of the 3rd platoon was Captain Vlajko Todorcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the 1st platoon, is this the officer platoon?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. It this was the first platoon composed of officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How was your company deployed in combat in accordance with the training that you had undergone, the objective, and had this unit received the training for this kind of combat?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of October, in fact, the unit was meant to be used to fight terrorist formations. It was organised in this way that if you have a terrorist group, the elements of this unit were supposed to encircle it and then the broader encirclement should be done by the soldier platoon and then my unit should go in and destroy the group. In Vukovar, when we entered combat, I received the task to take the soldiers's element of our unit, the two soldier platoons, to be as part of the 2nd Infantry Battalion, to cover their backs, so to speak, and to prevent any attacks by Croatian units that could be expected to be launched from the underground tunnels that were rumoured to have existed. So if any such actions were launched, I was to prevent them; and if, in their advance, they should come to a stronghold, I was supposed to deal with it. And if the stronghold was particularly strong, then the first platoon that was in Negoslavci as some kind of a reserve would be engaged. That was -- it was there at the brigade headquarters. I think that the unit was not really meant to perform this kind of tasks. But at that time, it was justified to deploy it in this manner because we were -- we had the best training. These were the early days of the combat there, and it was only logical to deploy us in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you said that on the 2nd, you joined the fight and you described in which way. Can you please tell us who issued you the order to join the fight on the 2nd?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: I was given the direct order by Colonel Mrksic, who was the brigade commander. So it was on the 1st, around 10.00 p.m., that was in the brigade headquarters. He told me, Battalion Commander Kavalic, Branislav Kavalic. He was a major; he was present there. Colonel Mrksic told me the basic concept of the task and told me that I should report to Major Adem Bajic, the commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment deployed in the sector stretching from the Negoslavci, the village of Negoslavci, the outskirts of the village towards Vukovar. And he told me that I would be given a more detailed task by that person, and that's how it happened. At 2.00 a.m. -- Is it necessary for me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I just posed a very general question. So if you could give me very brief answers, until we get to the main point. On the 2nd of October, you took part in fighting. Why does that day stick in your memory, Mr. Maric? Is there anything particular that made you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the first time that I took part in fighting and that very fact makes it memorable. But I was also wounded that morning, so these are the two things that really -- the most basic things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So you were wounded on the 2nd of October. What happened then? Did you stay in Vukovar? Did you -- were you transported some place; and, if so, can you explain to us until when you were absent from Vukovar and from combat?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: I was wounded at around 8.00 a.m. I was given first aid in the Vukovar barracks, and then I was transported to the hospital in Negoslavci. I think it was about 10.00 or 11.00 when I came there, and then I was transferred to the military medical academy the same day in the evening of the same day. And I was there being treated until early November. I was first in the military medical academy and then I was at home, and then I returned -- I don't know the exact date, the 5th, the 10th, sometime in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were transferred to the VMA, military medical academy?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where it is? We all know that but for the same of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: It is located in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please wait until I finish my question and then give your answer, Mr. Maric. While you were absent from the 2nd of October until your return to Vukovar, which was sometime between the 5th and the 10th of November, 1991, who was in command of the company -- military police company, I mean the anti-terrorist company?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: While I was absent, the company was under the command of Captain Todorcic, that was the soldier element; and the officer element was commanded by (redacted). And the person in overall control was Captain Susic, because he was the deputy commander of the battalion so he had the command of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: During your treatment for your injury and during your absence from Vukovar, did you get any information about the situation in your unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: I got most of my information from the wounded, who would come into the military medical academy while I was there, and the people that I visited when I was discharged from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I will not now ask you about what happened when you returned. What I'm interested in is something else. Do you remember when Vukovar was liberated from our -- from this perspective, some people say it was occupied on that date. Can you tell us the date; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: It was the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you -- I mean, your unit had any tasks on the 18th of November, 1991, and what were those tasks?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, our task was to secure the left wing of the 2nd Assault Detachment that was attacking the Stjepan Zupanc school and to continue on along the axis towards the high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And did you execute this task?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This task was executed between 10.00 a.m., when the action started, until 1500 hours when we reached the water tower area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain. The water tower area, where is this area in Vukovar? What is it adjacent to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: The water tower is on a ridge, and there is the church there, the high school, and the water tower. These are the landmarks there. And we were actually attacking eastwards, and there is the Danube River that is behind this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any combat in this area on the 18th, and did something specific happen there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no direct clashes. We were just advancing, and we did not encounter any resistance. The specific thing is that there were many civilians there. As we advanced, they would come out of the shelters, and this was the impression that I got. I never expected that many people to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th, did you learn anything about what was going on at Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Nothing special, nothing particular. We were progressing along our axis. Later in the afternoon, sometime after noon, we learned that one unit had surrendered commanded by Crni or Veliki Joe. I am not sure, that was the nickname of that person. It was the so-called Mitnica unit, and this is what we took to be the end of the operation aimed at liberating Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you mentioned a large number of civilians, could you explain to us where did those civilians emerge from?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Along the axis that my unit took to the left, there is a hillock with many wine cellars, I presume. A large number of people emerged from there; and in the area of the water tower, there were many wine cellars dug into the earth and a large number of people emerged from those as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do with these civilians, Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: We forwarded those civilians, pursuant to orders given, down that street. I do not recall the name of the street, where there were accosted by a military police unit that was behind us, who then directed them to a prearranged place for that purpose. I believe that that place was Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, do you recall that you had a meeting with a member of Croatian paramilitary units during the 18th, during carrying out your operations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: When we reached the water tower, we hoisted our flag on the water tower. It was to signal the point to which we advanced, and that water tower is in the immediate vicinity of Mitnica. And coming from Mitnica, there was a member of Croatian forces who wore a camouflage blouse. He was armed, but he wore civilian trousers. We disarmed him. We, (redacted) and I, disarmed him. And while waiting for a vehicle to arrive to take him to a certain place, I entered into conversation with him. He told me that that his name was Herve [phoen] Djako. He used to be a butcher; he was a manager of a supermarket. We discussed matters, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Maric, you said that you were waiting for a vehicle to take this man. Do you know what happened to him later on, who he was handed over to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: I know that he was exchanged; and before that, he was taken to Velepromet. He was exchanged when the members of such units were exchanged. I was told that by my superior officer who managed and oversaw that exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When did you accomplish your operation that you started with on at 10.00?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: I completed it when the dusk fell. We had secured the line, because Mitnica had not been inspected and searched. And when dusk fell, I went back to my observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. You came back to your observation post after dusk had fallen. Did you receive any other tasks while you were there; if so, from who and what kind of a task?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Sometime later, maybe one hour after my arrival to the observation post, I received from Colonel Mrksic a task to go to the Ovcara region, where the surrendered combatants were, to inspect whether everything was all right there, to perform a security assessment, and to report back on my findings to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go there, and what was the composition of the group that you took there? Could you tell us approximately what time it was?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: I took three vehicles together with officers, some 20 of them. I believe that we reached Ovcara at around 8.00 p.m. It's very difficult for me to pinpoint time, but I believe that it was around 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is the same commissioned officers, platoon, that had been involved in your operation earlier that day?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had no other such platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was the komandir of that commissioned officers platoon there. I'm not going to name him for obvious reasons?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain, Mr. Maric, your arrival to Ovcara: What you saw, what you did, how long you were there? Just proceed slowly with your description. If need be, I'm going to ask you additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Since I had never been to Ovcara before and it was dark already, we proceeded in the following manner. Komandir of the platoon would take his vehicle in front of me. I was in the middle and the third brought up the rear. When we reached Ovcara, there are no other facilities en route. It was dark. We stopped in front of a warehouse. To our right, as we approached, the door was open. On a plateau, there was a Pinzgauer vehicle with headlights on, parked at a slant, and the headlights provided lighting for the interior of the warehouse. There was some soldiers standing by the Pinzgauer wearing olive drab or JNA uniforms. We got out of our vehicles, and I asked, "Who is the commanding officer here?" Some lieutenant-colonel was there. He was shorter than me, wore a moustache. He told me his name, but I did not remember it. I asked him what was going on there, and he briefly told me that the prisoners were there, that nothing particular was going on. We had a short discussion, and then I went into the hangar. I entered the hangar to make sure that there were -- whether there were any of my former soldiers or subordinates in there. The situation was like this: To the right-hand side, there was a rope stretched a certain distance. There were 70, 80 people. I could not see very well. It was quite dark. The only lighting came from the headlights. When we came in, the people withdrew towards the back wall out of fear, and I regretted my coming in immediately. And after I made some headway, five, six metres into the hangar, there were some soldiers kneeling down spaced at five, six metres. They were guarding the prisoners. Opposite the entrance, I saw something that I thought might be illegal. I approached them to ask them what was going on. There was one soldiers -- or one prisoner who was urinating. And then I heard behind me one member of Croatian forces, to the effect that he was protesting that they had been promised to be treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. One of my officers tersely ordered him to go back to where he came from, and then I ordered my men to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I apologise for interrupting you. You said that on your right-hand side from the entrance, there was 70, 80 prisoners. Opposite them, there were four to five soldiers with rifles trained at them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: They were not trained at them; they were just guarding them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What was the distance between the rope and the people?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe ten to 15 metres, as wide as this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from these people behind the rope and the soldiers guarding them, was there anybody else on that evening on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay here?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: For half an hour, maybe an hour at most. But let me tell you another thing. After emerging from the hangar, maybe four or five of my people followed me in. The rest inspected the surrounds of the facility and reported back to me that there was nothing around the facility, that everything was calm. And I reported to Colonel Mrksic that my assessment was that everything was in order there, that there was no need for me to stay on there at that facility, and then Mr. Mrksic told us, "Then get some rest."

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The order for this task you received from Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you inform your immediate superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Captain Susic. I informed him upon my return that I had completed that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said that next to the vehicle providing lighting for the hangar, that there was one lieutenant-colonel. Did you contact him, discuss possible problems at the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had another conversation for a while after I emerged from the hangar; and when my people came back to report to me, we discussed that there was nothing else around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did that lieutenant-colonel say that there were any problems?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he expected some problems?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He thought that something might happen, in terms that it's dark. There were cornfields around, that there may be some combat action, but that was his assessment rather than a reflection of reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you offer him any assistance, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I gave him the radio frequency where I may be contacted at, and I told him that if he had any other problems that he may contact me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So you departed after one hour from the hangar at Ovcara, so that could be around 9.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. 9.00 p.m., plus/minus half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything interesting around Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a commotion; there was a crowd of civilians emerging from Vukovar, some buses. Lieutenant-Colonel Vukasinovic was marshalling people around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What was that distance between that place and the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Some 100, 150 metres, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After that, you came back to your observation post?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. My whole unit came back with me to my observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like us to conclude because the next topic is the 19th, which I cannot process in two minutes' time. So if we may continue tomorrow, I would be much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Bulatovic. We must adjourn now, then, and we resume tomorrow at 9.30, and the evidence of the witness will continue then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of November, 2006, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.59 p.m.,
